comparison_markdown:
# Hotjar vs OpenReplay

## Overview

Behavior analytics tool with heatmaps, session recordings, and surveys. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. OpenReplay is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Hotjar costs Free / $32-$80+/month; OpenReplay is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: Hotjar is Proprietary; OpenReplay is AGPL 3.0
- **Data ownership**: OpenReplay can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: OpenReplay eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: OpenReplay has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Hotjar | OpenReplay |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $32-$80+/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Hotjar

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### OpenReplay

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [openreplay/openreplay](https://github.com/openreplay/openreplay) * ~9k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Hotjar if:** Hotjar is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose OpenReplay if:** OpenReplay is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Hotjar in its standard export format, review OpenReplay import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

OpenReplay is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Hotjar tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your OpenReplay instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Hotjar, switching to self-hosted OpenReplay will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Hotjar until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Hotjar paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is OpenReplay free to use?
Yes. OpenReplay is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Hotjar to OpenReplay?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Hotjar data, follow the OpenReplay import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does OpenReplay get regular updates?
Yes. OpenReplay has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use OpenReplay without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if OpenReplay development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Hotjar](https://hotjar.com) and [OpenReplay](https://openreplay.com) before making decisions.*

title: Loom vs Cap
comparison_markdown:
# Loom vs Cap (2026)

## Overview
Loom and Cap are both video recording and sharing tools that help teams communicate more effectively. This comparison is useful for teams looking to switch from a proprietary, cloud-based solution like Loom to a self-hosted, open-source alternative like Cap. The core use case for both tools is to enable easy video recording and sharing, and teams may switch to Cap to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Loom charges $12.50-$14.99 per user per month, while Cap is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: Loom stores user data on its proprietary servers, while Cap allows users to host their own data on their own servers.
* Setup complexity: Loom is generally easier to set up, with a simpler onboarding process, while Cap requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Cap is more scalable than Loom, as users can simply add more server resources as needed.
* Integration: Loom has a more comprehensive integration with popular project management tools like Asana and Trello, while Cap has a more limited set of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Loom | Cap |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $12.50-$14.99/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $12.50-$14.99/user/month = $625-$749.50/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $12.50-$14.99/user/month = $2,500-$2,998/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Loom:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Comprehensive integrations with popular tools
* Good customer support
* Limited control over user data
* Can be expensive for large teams
**Cap:**
* Free and self-hosted
* Highly scalable
* Users have full control over their data
* Limited integrations with popular tools
* Can be complex to set up and maintain

## When to Choose Each
Loom is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that need a simple, easy-to-use video recording and sharing tool, and are willing to pay a premium for convenience and good customer support. Cap, on the other hand, is a good choice for larger teams or organizations that need a high degree of control over their data and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining a self-hosted solution.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Loom videos in MP4 format.
2. Set up a Cap server and configure it to your needs.
3. Use the Cap import tool to upload your Loom videos to your Cap server.
4. Update any links or integrations to point to your new Cap server.

## Our Take
Cap is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the polish and features of Loom. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Cap's video encoding and playback can be slower than Loom's, especially for larger videos. However, for teams that value data ownership and scalability, Cap is a good choice, and we recommend switching if you have a large team and don't need all the bells and whistles of Loom.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams that don't need integrations with popular project management tools
* Large teams that need to reduce costs and increase scalability
* Teams that value data ownership and control
* Organizations with strict data security requirements
* Teams that are already self-hosting other tools and want to add video recording and sharing to their stack

## FAQ
### Can I use Cap for free?
Yes, Cap is free and self-hosted, which means you can use it at no cost beyond the cost of hosting your own server.
### Is Cap as easy to use as Loom?
No, Cap can be more complex to set up and use, especially for non-technical users.
### Can I integrate Cap with popular project management tools?
Not yet, Cap's integrations are still limited, but the developers are working on adding more.
### How do I migrate my Loom videos to Cap?
You can export your Loom videos in MP4 format and then use the Cap import tool to upload them to your Cap server.
### Is Cap production-ready?
Not yet, Cap is still a relatively new tool and may not be suitable for all users, especially those who need a high degree of polish and features.
meta_description: Cap, a free self-hosted video recording tool, vs Loom. See full comparison or Free migration guide.

title: Sketch vs Penpot
comparison_markdown:
# Sketch vs Penpot (2026)

## Overview
Sketch and Penpot are two popular design tools used for user interface (UI) and user experience (UX) design. This comparison is beneficial for designers, developers, and product managers who want to choose the best tool for their design needs. The core use case for both tools is to create and collaborate on design projects, and the key reason someone would switch is to take advantage of Penpot's free and self-hosted options.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Sketch offers a subscription-based model, while Penpot is free and open-source.
* Data ownership: Penpot allows users to self-host and have full control over their data, whereas Sketch stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Sketch has a more straightforward setup process, while Penpot requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Penpot is more scalable due to its open-source nature and self-hosting capabilities.
* Feature difference: Penpot has a more extensive library of plugins and integrations, including support for Figma files, whereas Sketch has a more limited set of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Sketch | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $9-$20/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $450-$1000/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1800-$4000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Sketch:**
* Easy to use and intuitive interface
* Large community of users and designers
* Seamless integration with other Sketch tools
* Regular updates with new features
* Limited scalability and control over data
**Penpot:**
* Free and open-source
* Self-hosting capabilities for full data control
* Extensive library of plugins and integrations
* Highly scalable and customizable
* Steeper learning curve due to technical requirements

## When to Choose Each
Sketch is suitable for small to medium-sized design teams who prioritize ease of use and a large community of users. It's ideal for teams who don't require full control over their data and are willing to pay a subscription fee. On the other hand, Penpot is perfect for larger teams or organizations that require scalability, customization, and full control over their data. It's also suitable for teams who are technically inclined and want to take advantage of its free and self-hosted options.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Sketch files in the JSON format.
2. Use the Penpot import tool to upload your JSON files.
3. Review and adjust your designs to ensure compatibility with Penpot.
4. Set up your Penpot account and configure your self-hosting options if desired.
5. Invite your team to collaborate on your designs in Penpot.

## Our Take
Penpot is not yet production-ready for most users due to its technical requirements and limited support resources. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Penpot's performance can be affected by the size and complexity of your designs. However, for teams who are technically inclined and require full control over their data, Penpot is a great alternative to Sketch.

## Who Should Switch
* Small design teams who don't require advanced features and want to save on costs
* Large enterprises who need scalability and customization
* Teams who require full control over their data and want to self-host
* Freelance designers who want to use a free and open-source tool
* Teams who don't need seamless integration with other Sketch tools

## FAQ
### Can I use Penpot for free?
Yes, Penpot is free and open-source, and you can self-host it to have full control over your data.
### Is Penpot compatible with Figma files?
Yes, Penpot supports Figma files and allows you to import and edit them.
### Can I use Penpot for large-scale design projects?
Yes, Penpot is highly scalable and suitable for large-scale design projects.
### Does Penpot have a user-friendly interface?
Penpot's interface is not as intuitive as Sketch, but it's still user-friendly and customizable.
### Is Penpot suitable for non-technical users?
No, Penpot is not suitable for non-technical users due to its technical requirements and limited support resources.
meta_description: Penpot, a free and self-hosted design tool, offers scalability and customization. See full comparison or Free migration guide.

* Cost: Figma offers a free plan with limited features, while Inkscape is completely free and open-source.

* Setup Complexity: Figma has a more streamlined setup process, while Inkscape requires more technical expertise to set up and customize.
* Scalability: Figma is more scalable and suitable for large teams, while Inkscape is better suited for individuals or small teams.
* Feature Difference: Figma has a more comprehensive set of collaboration features, while Inkscape has more advanced vector editing capabilities.

| Aspect | Figma | Inkscape |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $12-$75/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | GPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |

| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2400-$15000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

### Figma
* Pros:
	+ Streamlined collaboration features
	+ Scalable and suitable for large teams
	+ Comprehensive design capabilities
	+ Cloud-based storage and automatic backups
	+ Integrates with other design tools and services
* Cons:
	+ Expensive, especially for large teams
	+ Limited control over data storage and ownership
	+ Dependent on internet connection
### Inkscape
* Pros:
	+ Free and open-source
	+ Advanced vector editing capabilities
	+ Customizable and extensible
	+ Stores files locally for greater control and security
	+ Cross-platform compatibility
* Cons:
	+ Steeper learning curve
	+ Limited collaboration features
	+ Not as scalable as Figma

Figma is the better choice for large teams or organizations that require streamlined collaboration features and scalable design capabilities. It is also suitable for individuals or teams who prioritize ease of use and are willing to pay for a cloud-based design tool. On the other hand, Inkscape is the better choice for individuals or small teams who prioritize data ownership and control, and are looking for a free and customizable design tool. It is also suitable for users who require advanced vector editing capabilities and are willing to invest time in learning the tool.

## Migration Path
1. Export Figma design files in SVG format.
2. Import SVG files into Inkscape using the built-in import tool.
3. Adjust and customize the design as needed to take advantage of Inkscape's advanced vector editing capabilities.
4. Set up a self-hosted solution for storing and collaborating on design files.
5. Update workflows and processes to accommodate the new design tool and collaboration features.

We recommend switching to Inkscape if you are an individual or small team looking for a free and customizable design tool, and are willing to invest time in learning the tool and setting up a self-hosted solution.
